article_title: Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition (CIRC) — Adolescent Literacy
citation: Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report, Adolescent Literacy. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Cooperative paired and small-group literacy routines with team rewards
description: CIRC's instructional pattern organises daily lessons around cooperative structures: "Pairs of students read to each other; predict how stories will end; summarize stories; write responses to questions posed by the teacher; and practice spelling, decoding, and vocabulary". Within teams of four, mixed-ability students work on story main ideas and linked writing activities, and teams are rewarded on collective performance to motivate helping. The pattern integrates comprehension practice with the writing process on the texts students read.
requirements: Teacher training in cooperative learning strategies and program management, provided via the two-day session described in the report
constraints: Implemented in the reviewed studies with grades 2–6 students in US elementary schools
target_learners: upper elementary and middle-grade students in mixed-ability classrooms
examples: The program description states that within cooperative teams of four, students work to understand the main idea of a story and work through linked writing activities, with rewards based on team performance

article_title: Tough As Nails and Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia
citation: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs
title: Ground research and education design in civic imagination because people cannot work toward a future they cannot see
description: Drawing on Jenkins and Shresthova's civic imagination rationale, the presentation holds that inclusive research must help communities envision futures before pursuing them. Its first rationale states: "People can't work toward a future if they can't see it first", illustrated by contrasting circa-1993 career horizons (teacher, miner, nurse) with emerging regional possibilities such as entrepreneurship, eco-tourism, agtech, and computing careers.
requirements: Research and pathway design must surface and make visible plausible future careers and identities for the community
constraints: Framed for communities like coal-transitioning Appalachia where prior career horizons were narrow
target_learners: K-8 students and their teachers in Eastern Kentucky
target_learning_goals: Envisioning future educational and career possibilities
examples: Slides contrast circa-1993 career options with 2023-and-beyond options including computing, eco-tourism, and agtech
key_sources: Emi Iwatani. (2023). Tough as Nails & Drawing on Kinship: Rigorous and inclusive educational research in Kentucky Appalachia [Invited speaker session]. American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting, Chicago, IL. https://bit.ly/TANrefs

article_title: State Support for Civic Engagement
citation: Thompson, C. (2023). State support for civic engagement. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/878.726
title: Civic diploma seals as a state pattern for recognizing student civic readiness
description: The report describes a growing state pattern of recognizing civic engagement through seals on students' diplomas. Seven states (Arizona, California, Georgia, Nevada, New York, Ohio, and Virginia) offer such a seal in the 2022-23 school year, and Tennessee offers one for districts or schools. In the seven student-seal states, "all require students to complete service learning, community service, or civic action, combined with course requirements," and LEAs validate requirements, confer seals, and report data to the state education agency. The National Council for the Social Studies has developed a toolkit supporting states interested in developing civic seals.
requirements: Local education agencies must validate requirements, confer seals, and report attainment data to the state education agency
constraints: Seals are optional additions to a traditional diploma in states such as Arizona and Georgia
target_learners: High school students
examples: Arizona requires a 3.0 GPA in social studies, passing the Arizona Civics Exam, three civic learning programs, two civic engagement activities, and 75 or more hours of community service
key_sources: Thompson, C. (2023). State support for civic engagement. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/878.726

article_title: Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing
citation: Brian Wright. (2026). Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25303
title: Treat citation-traceability as a deployment requirement for classroom AI tools in machine learning courses
description: The article argues that what matters pedagogically is not just answer correctness but whether "a claim can be traced back to the lecture, slide, or reading that introduced it." A fluent, plausible, ungrounded answer is the more dangerous classroom failure mode because it short-circuits the student's check against source material, whereas a wrong-but-checkable answer keeps the student positioned as the one doing the checking. The author suggests this could argue for treating citation-traceability as a deployment requirement rather than an optional feature, and notes it could help develop trust in the emerging Teacher-Student-LLM dynamic in machine learning classrooms.
requirements: The knowledge representation must preserve where content originated and let a student follow any claim back to its source, as the compiled wiki's citations do.
constraints: The article states further testing is needed before generalizing; the groundedness evidence comes from a single-run evaluation on one course corpus, not from classroom deployments with students.
target_learners: undergraduate machine learning students
instructors teaching machine learning courses
target_learning_goals: students verifying AI tutor claims against course source materials
keeping students positioned as the ones doing the checking rather than outsourcing judgment to the tool
examples: In the evaluation, the compiled wiki's citations let a student and instructor trace any claim back to the lecture that introduced it, and the wiki arm was grounded in 98% of answers versus 81% for vector RAG.
key_sources: Brian Wright. (2026). Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25303

article_title: Artificial intelligence in vocational education and training: A systematic review of educational purposes, theoretical conceptualizations, and empirical effectiveness
citation: Deutscher, V., Thomann, H., Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia, O., Weyland, U., Abele, S., Danek, A. H., Greiff, S., Rausch, A., Seeber, S., Seifried, J., & Winther, E. (2026). Artificial intelligence in vocational education and training: A systematic review of educational purposes, theoretical conceptualizations, and empirical effectiveness. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100628. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100628
title: Curriculum-Instruction-Assessment triad taxonomy of AI educational purposes in VET
description: Building on Wang et al. (2024) and Dai et al. (2025), the review organizes AI applications in VET "into the main categories of the Curriculum-Instruction-Assessment-Triad (Pellegrino, 2012)", plus holistic system-level functions. The curriculum domain covers curriculum creation and analysis; the instruction domain distinguishes seven pedagogical functions (instructional planning, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, conversational agents, content curation, instructional creation, authentic simulation); the assessment domain covers intelligent assessment and profiling/prediction; holistic functions include administration and guidance. Table 1 maps each purpose to AI types (ML, NLP, rule-based, computer vision) and example applications.
requirements: The taxonomy requires classifying each AI application by educational purpose, AI type, and example application, as operationalized in the review's coding scheme and Appendix 1.
constraints: The review found instructional applications dominate the evidence base while curriculum- and assessment-oriented uses remain marginal, and it excluded AI as a learning object (AI literacy) from scope.
target_learners: vocational education and training learners
target_learning_goals: mapping AI applications to educational purposes in vocational contexts
examples: Conversational agents were the most prevalent instructional subcategory (ten studies); iXR accounted for eight studies; profiling and prediction appeared in two dropout-risk studies.

article_title: Review of the effects of citizenship education
citation: E. Geboers, F. Geijsel, W. Admiraal, G. ten Dam. (2013). Review of the effects of citizenship education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2012.02.001
title: Two-domain organization of citizenship: political and social domains
description: The review organizes students' citizenship into at least two domains, the political and the social, and uses this distinction to characterize the empirical literature it surveys. It reports that "the political domain of citizenship to be emphasized more than the social domain," indicating that research on citizenship education has concentrated on political aspects of citizenship while giving comparatively less attention to social aspects. The framework serves as the review's organizing axis for describing what citizenship education effects concern.
requirements: Empirical studies of citizenship education must specify which domain of citizenship their outcomes concern for the domain distinction to be applied.
constraints: The review's corpus of 2003-2009 studies emphasized the political domain more than the social domain, so evidence on social-domain outcomes is comparatively limited.
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: citizenship development in political and social domains

article_title: The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization
citation: Huatong Sun. (2006). The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization. Technical Communication Quarterly, 15(4), 457-481. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1504_5
title: Circuit of culture: five interlocking processes (representation, identity, production, consumption, regulation) for examining a cultural artifact
description: Borrowed from British cultural studies (du Gay et al., 1997), the circuit of culture examines "five key processes in a development cycle of an artifact": how the artifact is represented, what social identities are associated with it, how it is produced, how it is consumed, and what mechanisms regulate its distribution and use. In the real world these five elements continually overlap and intertwine in complex and contingent ways. Applied to usability, it shows how representation, identity, production, and regulation interact with and contribute to consumption, providing a timeline and developmental perspective missing from activity theory and genre theory.
requirements: A study of the whole circuit of culture is needed to examine a cultural artifact completely
constraints: The five elements overlap and intertwine in complex and contingent ways rather than forming a linear sequence
target_learners: usability researchers
IT product designers
localization specialists
target_learning_goals: analyzing how meanings are mediated by an artifact across its full life cycle
examples: The author maps mobile text messaging onto the circuit, locating developer localization in production and user localization across consumption, regulation, representation, and identity

article_title: Metacognition and self-regulation in young children: does it matter if metacognitive experiences are communicated?
citation: Ventura, Ana Clara. (2022). Metacognition and self-regulation in young children: does it matter if metacognitive experiences are communicated?. Early Years. https://doi.org/10.1080/09575146.2022.2065666
title: C.Ind.Le Coding Scheme-based coding of metacognitive knowledge, regulation, emotional and motivational regulation, and spontaneous FOD comments
description: The study's measurement approach applies the C.Ind.Le Coding Scheme to individual interviews of six-year-olds during an ecological and challenging graphic task. It codes "indicators of metacognitive knowledge (i.e., knowledge of persons, tasks and strategies), metacognitive regulation (i.e., planning, monitoring, control and evaluation) and emotional and motivational regulation (i.e., emotional and motivational monitoring and control)", plus children's spontaneous comments of feelings of difficulty.

target_learners: young children (six-year-old first graders)
examples: Applied with sixty first graders (57% boys; M age: 6.2 yr., SD = 3 months) individually interviewed during the graphic task

article_title: Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games
citation: Taehyun Kim, Mike Tissenbaum. (2025). Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09459-2
title: City Settlers: a hybrid game-based simulation for whole-class science learning
description: City Settlers is a browser-based, whole-room simulation in which small teams manage and grow cities on a shared planet, engaging both digital and in-person interaction. "In this game-based simulation, there are five key components: resources, trading, buildings, auctions, and city status." constraints: The game was purpose-built rather than commercial, designed to let students explore the rise and fall of cities belonging to local Indigenous peoples, with no imposed winning conditions.

article_title: Living the DReaM: The interrelations between statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainty articulations through citizen science
citation: Aridor, K., Dvir, M., Tsybulsky, D., & Ben-Zvi, D. (2023). Living the DReaM: The interrelations between statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainty articulations through citizen science. Instr Sci, 51, 729–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09626-8
title: Citizen science as a context for concurrently fostering statistical, scientific and NOS reasoning
description: The article positions citizen science as a pedagogical design pattern in which learners engage in authentic scientific practices, including data analysis, while learning scientific content. It states: 'The context of Citizen Science is particularly suited for this goal, providing a unique pedagogical opportunity for learning scientific content by engaging learners in authentic scientific practices, including data analysis.' The Radon Citizen Science Project learning sequence operationalized this pattern.

constraints: Pilot implementation was partially inhibited by COVID-19 restrictions

target_learning_goals: appreciating the role of uncertainty in generating data-based scientific knowledge
examples: Radon Citizen Science Project learning sequence in which students conducted radon surveys and analyzed data

article_title: Advances in research on composite instructional designs – investigating intermediate knowledge and preparation effects
citation: Katharina Loibl, Valentina Nachtigall, Timo Leuders. (2025). Advances in research on composite instructional designs – investigating intermediate knowledge and preparation effects. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09751-6
title: The CID framework explains preparation effects in composite instructional designs through intermediate knowledge
description: The CID framework (a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs) explains how learning in one phase affects subsequent phases by focusing on the learner's knowledge state between phases. The editorial states it analyzes "intermediate knowledge"—the knowledge between phases—and how it shapes further learning, constituting a preparation effect. It builds on Koedinger et al. (2012) by positing analysis on three levels: instructional design, learning processes, and knowledge components, supported by research designs that isolate single mechanisms.
requirements: A well-crafted research design that helps to isolate single mechanisms, and analysis on three levels—instructional design, learning processes, and knowledge components
constraints: Studying only the sequence of phases tests general effects, not single mechanisms; the framework recommends additionally manipulating one phase without altering the sequence
target_learners: learners in formal instructional settings across domains
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and transfer in multi-phase instructional designs
examples: The editorial links all special-issue contributions to the framework, including studies altering phase sequence and studies manipulating a single phase
key_sources: Katharina Loibl, Valentina Nachtigall, Timo Leuders. (2025). Advances in research on composite instructional designs – investigating intermediate knowledge and preparation effects. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09751-6

article_title: Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students’ engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction
citation: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7
title: Collaborative information processing (CIP) model: externalization, divergence and convergence phases of collaborative knowledge building
description: The article invokes Jorczak's collaborative information processing model, which "distinguishes three phases of collaborative information processing that develop cyclically in the processes of negotiation and collaborative knowledge building: externalization, divergence and convergence". Externalization expresses stored knowledge to share it; in divergence learners elaborate and compare ideas to identify discrepancies; in convergence learners negotiate and resolve socio-cognitive discrepancies. The authors use CIP to interpret summary dyads as typically not going beyond externalization.
requirements: Requires processes of negotiation and collaborative knowledge building among learners
target_learners: secondary education students working in dyads
examples: The authors conclude that pairs who jointly wrote a summary did not, in general, go beyond the initial externalization phase
key_sources: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7

article_title: CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs
citation: Katharina Loibl · Timo Leuders · Inga Glogger-Frey · Nikol Rummel. (2025). CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09665-9
title: CID framework linking knowledge, learning, and instruction levels across phases of composite instructional designs
description: The CID framework extends the knowledge–learning–instruction approach to multi-phase designs. As the authors state, it is "a framework for conductin g cognitive analyses of composite instructional designs (CID) that links the three levels – (K) knowledge components, (L) learning processes, and (I) instructional designs". Its core element is intermediate knowledge (K1) generated by the first phase, which shapes learning processes in the second phase; modelling prior knowledge (K0) additionally allows explanation of aptitude-treatment-interactions such as expertise-reversal effects.
requirements: Specification of the framework elements (K0, K1, K2, L1, L2, I1, I2) for a concrete instructional design to derive testable predictions
constraints: The general framework is, in the authors' words citing Anderson, "insufficiently specified to enable predictions to be derived" until elements are specified per design
The analyses focus primarily on cognitive dimensions; affective-motivational states are modelled only in parallel and rarely considered so far
target_learners: All learners in multi-phase instructional settings
target_learning_goals: Understanding mechanisms of composite instructional designs across phases
examples: Applied to Rau et al. (2017), Loibl and Rummel (2014), and Glogger-Frey et al. (2015, 2017) to explain preparatory, order, and contradictory effects
key_sources: Katharina Loibl · Timo Leuders · Inga Glogger-Frey · Nikol Rummel. (2025). CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09665-9

article_title: Can failure be made productive also in Bayesian reasoning? A conceptual replication study
citation: Loibl, K., & Leuders, T. (2024). Can failure be made productive also in Bayesian reasoning? A conceptual replication study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09670-y
title: CID framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs
description: The CID framework (cognitive analyses of composite instructional designs) is presented as "a useful means to systematically describe the elements of such an instructional design and its theoretical assumptions" for multi-phase designs like PS-I. It requires theoretical specification on the levels of knowledge, learning, and instruction, and introduces the notion of intermediate knowledge acquired in the first phase, which can alter learning processes in the second phase and thereby affect outcomes. The article uses it to align the replication's materials and mechanisms with the original study.
requirements: A theoretical specification on the levels of knowledge, learning, and instruction for each phase of the composite design
constraints: Designed for composite (multi-phase) instructional designs, extending single-phase frameworks such as KLI
target_learners: students in instructional-design research, e.g., undergraduate teacher students
target_learning_goals: conceptual and procedural knowledge of a target concept such as Bayesian reasoning or variance
examples: The article analyzes PS-I and I-PS sequences with the CID framework in Fig. 1 and uses it to structure the comparison of the original and replication studies (Tables 1 and 2)

article_title: Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer
citation: Saba, J., Kapur, M., & Roll, I. (2025). Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer. Instructional Science, 53, 1603–1632. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09726-7
title: Composite Instructional Design (CID) framework: intermediate knowledge links exploration phases to subsequent instruction
description: The CID framework, introduced by Loibl et al. (2024), provides "a structured lens for interpreting how the sequence of instructional phases shapes the intermediate knowledge students acquire during exploration and impacts their cognitive processes during instruction". Its central construct is intermediate knowledge — the state of knowledge after the initial phase — which can include target-knowledge components, activated prior knowledge, erroneous knowledge requiring refutation, knowledge-gap awareness, and procedural knowledge. The framework holds that the effectiveness of subsequent direct instruction depends heavily on the intermediate knowledge and cognitive states fostered during prior exploration. This study uses CID to interpret Exploration-first versus Instruction-first sequences for MVC learning.
requirements: Instructional designs that combine multiple phases with different pedagogies and goals, so that an initial phase can foster intermediate knowledge that the subsequent phase builds on
constraints: The framework addresses designs combining multiple instructional phases; it was applied in this study to simulation-based exploration plus plenary instruction with undergraduates learning MVC
target_learners: undergraduate students in science and engineering programs
examples: The study interpreted Exploration-first exploration as fostering intermediate knowledge (prior-knowledge activation and knowledge-gap awareness) that the subsequent instruction phase built on through structured discussion and guided reflection

article_title: Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305
title: Critical interpretive synthesis underpinned by Kirkpatrick's return on investment model for reviewing workforce education effectiveness
description: This is the review's methodological framework: a "Critical interpretive synthesis underpinned by Kirkpatrick's return on investment model" applied to identify features of effective dementia educational programs. The approach integrates interpretive synthesis of heterogeneous studies with Kirkpatrick's evaluation framework, allowing the authors to judge program efficacy across training outcomes for the workforce.
requirements: Requires a corpus of studies on the educational interventions of interest, synthesised interpretively and evaluated against Kirkpatrick's return on investment model.
constraints: The authors note there remains limited understanding of how an informed and effective dementia workforce can be achieved, and that further robust research is required to develop the evidence base.
target_learners: Health and social care workforce staff receiving dementia education and training
target_learning_goals: Identifying features of effective dementia education and training programs
examples: The review applied this synthesis approach to 152 included papers of variable quality to derive the common features of more efficacious programs.

article_title: Advancing Contextual Interference: Addressing Methodological Debates, Reflecting on Meta-Analytic Practices and Generalizability, and Guiding Future Directions in Motor Learning
citation: Ammar, A., Trabelsi, K., Salem, A., Jahrami, H., & Schöllhorn, W. I. (2025). Advancing Contextual Interference: Addressing Methodological Debates, Reflecting on Meta-Analytic Practices and Generalizability, and Guiding Future Directions in Motor Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10043-1
title: The two-effect contextual interference hypothesis: high-CI practice yields inferior acquisition but superior retention and transfer
description: The contextual interference (CI) hypothesis holds that practice schedule structure produces two distinct effects: a first effect during acquisition and a second effect on relatively permanent learning. As the article states, the hypothesis "posits that high CI (e.g., random practice) leads to inferior acquisition (1st effect), but superior learning capabilities (2nd effect), operationalized in form of retention and/or transfer tests, compared to low CI (i.e., blocked practice)". The article uses this framework to organize its meta-analytic evaluations and to criticize reviews that analyze only the second effect while neglecting acquisition. It also notes serial practice lies conceptually between blocked and random formats, and that mechanisms such as elaboration and reconstruction are debated.
requirements: Studies must compare higher vs lower contextual interference practice conditions and measure acquisition plus retention and/or transfer outcomes
constraints: The article limits its synthesis to gross motor skills in applied sport and physical education settings
target_learners: learners of gross motor / sport skills in physical education and sports training
examples: The authors' meta-analyses evaluated outcome measures at post-test, retention and transfer, and computed changes across phases to capture both acquisition and relatively permanent gains

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective
citation: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2
title: Circumplex model of teachers' motivating styles organized by need support and directiveness
description: Teachers' motivating styles are depicted on a circumplex with two orthogonal dimensions: "the support, relative to the thwarting, of basic needs and the extent to which the teacher takes the lead and is directive or instead transfers the lead to students." The four quadrants represent four overarching teaching styles (autonomy support, structure, control, chaos), each divided into two subareas (attuning, participative; clarifying, guiding; domineering, demanding; awaiting, abandoning), for eight subareas total. Empirically, subareas correlate in sinusoidal patterns with outcomes, with peaks at need-supportive areas and decreasingly positive or negative correlations toward need-thwarting areas.
requirements: Measurement via the SIS vignette instrument (15 vignettes, 60 items) assessing the eight subareas
constraints: Validated previously in Belgian samples and here with Australian students; the demanding subarea's correlates were ambiguous in this data
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: motivation, engagement, and achievement in classroom learning
examples: Multidimensional scaling of SIS items confirmed the circular arrangement around the need-support and directiveness dimensions, comparable to previous research.

article_title: Examining the role of civic attitudes in the link between family wealth and school dropout among tertiary vocational students
citation: Finkenauer, C., Boer, M., Spitzer, J., Weinberg, D., Visser, K., Jonker, M. & Stevens, G. W. J. M. (2023). Examining the role of civic attitudes in the link between family wealth and school dropout among tertiary vocational students. npj Science of Learning 8:38. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00189-4
title: Civic attitudes account: institutional trust as the pathway linking experienced family wealth to school dropout
description: The article proposes that adolescents' civic attitudes — their beliefs about whether institutions are fair and can be trusted — explain part of the association between family wealth and school dropout. It distinguishes two related but distinct civic attitudes: institutional trust, which "focuses on the trustworthiness of specific institutions", and system justification, which "refers to beliefs about the overall fairness and legitimacy of the social, political, and economic systems in a specific country". In this account, experiencing financial scarcity lowers trust in institutions, which in turn reduces engagement and staying in school. The account is supported by the study's mediation models and framed as underexplored in dropout research.
requirements: Assessment of both objective family wealth and adolescents' own perceptions and experiences of wealth, since subjective experience is the operative predictor
constraints: Findings are correlational, with family wealth and civic attitudes assessed at the same timepoint, and were obtained in vocational schools in the Netherlands; generalization to other levels and countries is unclear

citation: Walsh, M. E., Lee-St. John, T. J., Raczek, A., & Foley, C. (2015). The long-term impact of systematic student support in elementary school: Reducing high school dropout. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED555563
title: City Connects systematic student support intervention with Site Coordinator and Practice Manual
description: City Connects is a systematic student support intervention currently implemented in 63 schools in Massachusetts, Ohio, and New York. At its core is a full-time Site Coordinator, a Masters'-trained school counselor or social worker, who collaborates with every classroom teacher to identify strengths and needs across four domains, connects students to a tailored set of community-based support services and enrichment opportunities, documents and tracks the service plan for each student, and follows up to assure service delivery and assess effectiveness. The model is codified in a Practice Manual with accompanying training and tools, including a proprietary electronic database for tracking service referral and delivery.
requirements: A full-time Site Coordinator who is a Masters'-trained school counselor or social worker
target_learners: Elementary school students in high-poverty urban districts
target_learning_goals: Addressing out-of-school barriers to achievement and thriving in school
examples: City Connects staff work with community agencies and families to deliver a tailored set of services to every child, with continuous assessment and follow up throughout the school year
key_sources: Walsh, M. E., Lee-St. John, T. J., Raczek, A., & Foley, C. (2015). The long-term impact of systematic student support in elementary school: Reducing high school dropout. SREE Spring 2015 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562544

article_title: The Effect of an Intensive English Program on Malaysian Secondary School Students' Language Proficiency
citation: Jayakaran Mukundan, Elaheh Hamed Mahvelati & Vahid Nimehchisalem. (2012). The Effect of an Intensive English Program on Malaysian Secondary School Students’ Language Proficiency. English Language Teaching, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p1
title: Certified Intensive English Program (CIEP) at ELS Language Centers
description: The CIEP is the core full-time proficiency course at ELS Language Centers Malaysia, structured into 9 levels grouped as Beginning (101–103), Intermediate (104–106), and Advanced (107–109). It runs full-time over 4 weeks per session (20 days), with 28 lessons per week covering "speaking, listening, reading, writing, pronunciation, vocabulary and gramma r". Components include Structure and Speaking Practice, Reading and Writing, Conversation, and E-Learning Language Technology (LTC).
requirements: Full-time attendance over a 4-week session (20 days), with 28 lessons per week of classroom instruction
constraints: Attendance requirements are very stringent: students were required not to miss class for more than 3 days
target_learners: Low-scoring Malaysian Form 4 secondary school students
target_learning_goals: General English language proficiency across listening, speaking, reading, and writing, plus grammar, spelling, and pronunciation
examples: In this study, 30 low-scoring students completed the CIEP at levels 101–105 at ELS Language Centers, Subang Jaya

title: Stress paradigm logic model: intervention components strengthen coping and adult relationships that buffer effects of urban poverty on academic and emotional-behavioral outcomes.
description: The article's logic model, grounded in the stress paradigm, holds that exposure to environmental stressors predicts negative outcomes and that protective processes, particularly coping skills and supportive adult relationships, can mitigate these effects. As the article states, "components of the developing intervention are expected to strengthen coping strategies and relationships with adults in the lives of adolescent participants in ways that buffer against the deleterious effects of stressors". Relationships with adults are expected to foster adaptive coping, which further strengthens relationships, extending beyond mentors to improve relationships with teachers and parents and thereby impact student engagement, achievement, and school completion.
requirements: Intervention components must strengthen both coping strategies and relationships with adults so the two mechanisms reinforce each other
constraints: The model is a theory of change; efficacy of the intervention had not yet been tested at the time of writing
target_learners: low-income urban middle school youth

title: Cities Mentor Project intervention components and timing.
description: Cities Mentor Project pairs 6th-grade students attending schools in low-income urban neighborhoods with university mentor-advocates who receive course credit and supervision through a service-learning course. Mentors and mentees attend coping training sessions after-school at partner schools administered by school-affiliated staff from a university-based community mental health center. Mentors connect with teachers and parents for academic advocacy, connect mentees to protective settings at partner community organizations, and practice coping strategies with mentees in real-life situations.

The program makes an eight-year commitment to youth with the plan to replace mentors as needed

target_learners: low-income urban middle school youth
examples: In Years 2 through 8, mentors and mentees attend booster coping training sessions, and mentors continue academic advocacy and connection to protective settings.

article_title: Relations between university teachers' teaching-related coping strategies and well-being over time: A cross-lagged panel analysis.
citation: Stockinger, K., Daumiller, M., & Dresel, M. (2026). Relations between university teachers' teaching‐related coping strategies and well‐being over time: A cross‐lagged panel analysis. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 54–72. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12777
title: Endler and Parker's task–emotion–avoidance coping taxonomy as a framework for teaching-related stress
description: The article adopts the Coping Inventory for Stressful Situations framework distinguishing "task‐oriented, emotion‐oriented and avoidance‐oriented coping" as broader strategy families for managing teaching-related stress. Task-oriented coping involves active engagement with stressors; emotion-oriented coping includes acceptance, relaxation, rumination, self-blame or resignation; avoidance-oriented coping involves cognitive or behavioural disengagement via distraction and social diversion. The study applies this taxonomy to university teachers' coping during remote teaching and notes a four-factor solution in which avoidance coping splits into distraction and social diversion.
requirements: Coping strategies are measured with the CISS-21 adapted to the teaching context, with items referencing stressful teaching situations over the past month
constraints: The three categories represent a higher-level functional organization; different ways of enacting these broader strategies can impact well-being in different ways, per the article
target_learners: university teachers and higher education teaching staff
target_learning_goals: managing teaching-related stress and emotions to support occupational well-being
examples: The study measured coping with the CISS-21 at two timepoints during the COVID-19 lockdown term, with avoidance coping modelled as two correlated facets, distraction and social diversion
key_sources: Stockinger, K., Daumiller, M., & Dresel, M. (2026). Relations between university teachers' teaching‐related coping strategies and well‐being over time: A cross‐lagged panel analysis. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 54–72. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12777

title: CI-CDSS: an EHR-integrated cognitive impairment clinical decision support system with electronic, paper, and interactive components
description: The CI-CDSS is a clinical decision support system embedded in an existing system-wide CDSS workflow, triggered by a web-service call at eligible visits for patients at risk of undetected CI. It "has three primary components: (1) an electronic risk-identification tool with diagnosis and care recommendations focused on brain health, (2) a paper version of the same tool, and (3) additional interactive tools and resources clinicians can click into via the EHR to guide diagnosis and care decisions." It supports detection, diagnosis, and post-diagnosis management of CI.
requirements: Requires integration into an existing EHR-based CDSS workflow that prints or displays content at eligible primary care visits
constraints: In the trial, self-reported receipt and use were modest and clicks into supplemental EHR resources occurred in only 1% of eligible visits
target_learners: Primary care clinicians caring for older adults
target_learning_goals: Detecting cognitive impairment risk at the point of care
Diagnosing and managing cognitive impairment care
examples: Implemented in 19 randomized clinics in August 2023; the paper tool was printed at 78% of eligible visits

citation: Yue Junyan, Shang Yun, Cui Hongkai, Liang Changhua, Wu Qingwu, Zhao Junqiang, Wang Huifang, Han Dongmin, Zhu Zhiping. (2025). title: Four-perspective CiteSpace scientometric framework for mapping CBL application in medical education
description: A scientometric analysis framework applying CiteSpace software (6.1.6R6) to visualize CBL research in Chinese and international medical education. It operates from four perspectives: "quantity analysis of literature; network analysis of co-occurring authors; network analysis of co-occurring research institutions; keywords clustering and burst analysis." The article uses it to compare Chinese and English corpora and proposes, on that basis, "a novel knowledge-oriented framework" aimed at enhancing effective CBL implementation in medical education.
requirements: Bibliographic corpora retrieved from defined databases (WoS core collection, CNKI, Wanfang, CQVIP) with deduplication via NoteExpress or CiteSpace
Data cleaning to standardize author names, countries, affiliations, and keywords
constraints: English-language literature is used to represent international medical education, so non-English international literature is outside its scope
High-frequency keywords do not necessarily pinpoint research hotspots with precision, as the article itself cautions
target_learners: medical education researchers and curriculum designers
target_learning_goals: understanding the research landscape and application state of case-based learning in medical education
examples: Analysis of 721 Chinese and 537 English articles (1995–2023) with time spans partitioned into 1-year slices, producing trend curves, co-author maps, institution maps, and keyword cluster/time diagrams

citation: Joyce P, Cunningham M, Alexander L. (2025). Evaluation of a hybrid model of a Physician Associate Studies programme: students, teachers, and examiner perspectives. Irish Journal of Medical Science 194(2):431-438. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11845-025-03918-3
title: CIPP (Context, Input, Process, Product) model as the evaluation framework for a hybrid programme innovation
description: The study used the Context, Input, Process, Product (CIPP) model as the framework to evaluate the hybrid PA programme. The article states it "provided a framework to establish the effectiveness and/or success of the hybrid model" and that it "particularly focuses on the inputs and process of an innovation". title: Circular multi-directional stitching training module with a GESEA-based scoring rubric and NASA-TLX workload measure
description: The study used a specially designed circular suturing training module with "four incisions in different directions on a slightly harder sponge material" and marked needle entry/exit points 0.5 cm in diameter, 0.75 cm from the incision. target_learning_goals: objective assessment of laparoscopic suturing quality and cognitive workload
examples: Scorers were blinded to participants and evaluated muted and de-identified videos; NASA-TLX was completed immediately after each task

article_title: Association of early bedtime at 3 years of age with higher academic performance and better non-cognitive skills in elementary school.
citation: Nishiyama Masahiro, Kyono Yuki, Yamaguchi Hiroshi, Kawamura Aoi, Oikawa Shizuka, Tokumoto Shoichi, Tomioka Kazumi, Nozu Kandai, Nagase Hiroaki. (2023). Association of early bedtime at 3 years of age with higher academic performance and better non-cognitive skills in elementary school. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-48280-5
title: Circadian rhythm account of why bedtime, rather than sleep duration, relates to childhood cognition
description: The article proposes an explanatory account in which the timing of sleep, not its total amount, matters for cognition because of circadian rhythm. It states that "bedtime, rather than sleep duration, was more associated with cognition, this may show the relevance of circadian rhythm", and reviews that circadian rhythm disturbance is common in neurodevelopmental disorders and that bright daytime light and avoidance of light at night increase circadian amplitude. Sleep duration did not correlate with future cognition in their data, which the authors read as indicating earlier-maturing individuals require less sleep.
requirements: The account presumes the observed bedtime–cognition association reflects circadian biology rather than unmeasured family factors, and rests on the cohort's null sleep-duration result.
constraints: The article states the results do not show that sleep in early childhood directly affects future academic or non-cognitive performance, and sleeping habits may reflect family economic, environmental, and genetic factors.
target_learners: children in early childhood (around 3 years of age)
target_learning_goals: academic performance in early elementary school
non-cognitive skills such as diligence and kindness
examples: The authors note decreased napping in preschool-aged children has been associated with higher cognition, suggesting it indicates biological brain maturation.

article_title: A rollercoaster of emotions: An integrative review of emotions and its impact on health professional students' learning in simulation-based education.
citation: Madsgaard, A., Smith‐Strøm, H., Hunskår, I., & Røykenes, K. (2022). A rollercoaster of emotions: An integrative review of emotions and its impact on health professional students' learning in simulation‐based education. Nursing Open, 9, 108–121. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1100
title: The circumplex model of affect as an organizing framework for emotions in simulation-based education
description: The review uses the circumplex model (CM) of affect as its organizing framework for classifying student emotions in SBE. The model "classifies emotions into two dimensions: valance and arousal", where valence is the experience of a situation as pleasant or unpleasant and arousal is the experience of being physiologically activated or deactivated. The review applies the model to interpret simulation emotions, noting that "High arousal activates the brain and this improves attention and memory" and that both negative and positive emotions can activate students in ways that benefit learning.
requirements: Emotions in a learning situation must be characterized along both the valence and arousal dimensions to apply the model
constraints: Valence has a complex impact on learning: positive emotions can broaden attention and cognition while negative emotions can promote deeper analytic processes
target_learners: Health professional students in simulation-based education
target_learning_goals: Understanding how emotions influence learning processes and outcomes in simulation
examples: The review categorized reported simulation emotions such as fear, anxiety and stress as negative and unpleasant according to the CM, and excitement, pride and enjoyment as activated emotions.
